clue.text: Has good intentions? Excellent, excellent!

blocks.note: slang: a mean cook is a very good one
swell is old-fashioned slang for excellent

explanation.surface: Someone cheers on hearing that a person has good intentions.
explanation.walkthrough: The two exclamations look like one repeated cheer, but each is a different slang word for very good.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean well is the idiom for having kindly purposes even if the result goes wrong; the question mark flags the phrase being split.

clue.text: Pot made by Spanish girl, broken by Spanish boy

indicators.note: something broken by another thing has that thing pushed into its middle

blocks.note: a typical Spanish girl's name
a typical Spanish boy's name

explanation.surface: A cooking pot made by a girl gets broken by a boy, both Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' reads as a cooking vessel; it is slang for the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Pot is a common slang term for cannabis, the drug also called marijuana.

clue.text: Snake in plant? Make off

indicators.note: telling something to be off means it is removed from the word

blocks.note: madder is a plant whose root gives a red dye
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A snake hides in a plant, and someone is told to get away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make off' looks like the phrase for running away; it means take the first letter of 'Make' off the plant's name, leaving the snake literally inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The adder is Britain's only venomous snake, a kind of viper.

clue.text: Slogan bandied about — 'spend money'

blocks.note: first meaning: a famous advertising catchphrase, widely repeated
second meaning: read literally, the words urge a passer-by to halt and make a purchase

explanation.surface: A catchy phrase going round that boils down to an urge to spend.
explanation.walkthrough: This was the slogan painted on Wall's ice-cream tricycles in Britain from the 1920s; taken at face value it is simply a call to buy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a well-known British advertising slogan whose literal message is an appeal to purchase.

clue.text: Remove from other court

blocks.note: extra means additional, other
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Someone is taken out of a different courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: To extract is to pull out or take away, as a dentist does with a tooth.

clue.text: Noble judge, one with millions in book

blocks.note: a lord is a nobleman
J is the abbreviation for judge
the Roman numeral for one
M is the abbreviation for million(s)

explanation.surface: A rich aristocratic judge appears as a character in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Jim is Joseph Conrad's 1900 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Jim is the title of a famous novel by Joseph Conrad, so it is an example of a book.

clue.text: South American tree producing a good deal of resin

indicators.note: a good deal of something is most but not all of it, so the word is cut short

blocks.note: balsam is an aromatic resin from trees

explanation.surface: A tropical tree yields plenty of resin.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last letter of the resin's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsa is a fast-growing tree of tropical America whose very light wood is used for models.

clue.text: Boy, moderately good in play

blocks.note: a boy's name
fair means middling, reasonably good

explanation.surface: A boy gives a moderately good performance in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Bartholomew Fair is a comedy by Ben Jonson, first staged in 1614.
explanation.definitionFit: Bartholomew Fair is a Jacobean comedy by Ben Jonson, so it is an example of a stage play.

clue.text: Girl cuddling boy in a state

indicators.note: to cuddle is to wrap one's arms round someone, so one name holds the other

blocks.note: a girl's name
a boy's name

explanation.surface: A girl hugs a boy who is upset and agitated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' reads as 'distressed', but 'a state' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisiana is one of the fifty states of the USA, on the Gulf of Mexico.

clue.text: A university study of British-born poet

blocks.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university
a den is a private room for study

explanation.surface: An academic study of a poet born in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: W.H. Auden was born in York and later became an American citizen, hence 'British-born'.
explanation.definitionFit: W.H. Auden was a major twentieth-century poet born in England who later took US citizenship.

clue.text: Drive in Beverly Hills? Went on horseback heading for ocean

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: rode is the past tense of ride
first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A famous shopping street, and someone riding a horse towards the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like a verb but is a street name; the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodeo Drive is the famous luxury shopping street in Beverly Hills, California, so the word completes the street's name.

clue.text: Go on stage and show them one's back!

blocks.note: your go is your turn in a game
a round is a stage of a competition

explanation.surface: A cheeky instruction to a performer to walk on and present their back to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on stage' reads as one theatrical phrase; it splits into two nouns, with 'on' simply placing one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotating to face the opposite direction presents one's back to whoever was in front.

clue.text: Prophet and saint's on film

blocks.note: an Old Testament prophet
St John, the apostle and evangelist
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prophet and a saint appear in a film.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremiah Johnson is a 1972 western starring Robert Redford.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeremiah Johnson is the title of a 1972 Robert Redford western, an example of a film.

clue.text: A reservoir worker refusing to be persuaded

blocks.note: taken as written
a dam holds back water and forms a reservoir
the worker ant is a crossword staple

explanation.surface: A waterworks employee who will not be talked round.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant describes someone utterly firm and unyielding in an opinion.

clue.text: Scaremongers unfortunately suppressing right film

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold down and keep in, so the outer word encloses the rest

blocks.note: alas is an exclamation of regret
R is the abbreviation for right
a thin film of moisture, as on a window

explanation.surface: People spreading fear have, sadly, managed to ban a proper film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests a movie but is a thin layer of condensation.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarmists are people who stir up needless fear, which is what scaremongers do.

clue.text: More than one teacher has changed on Hebridean island

indicators.note: something changed has its order altered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Mull is an island of the Inner Hebrides, off western Scotland
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Several teachers have been altered by life on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged word is placed after the island's name, which is what 'on' signals here.
explanation.definitionFit: A mullah is a Muslim scholar and teacher of religious law, so the plural means several teachers.

clue.text: Meets French composer touring island with fine son

indicators.note: a touring party goes all round a place, so one name surrounds the other letters

blocks.note: Erik Satie, French composer of the Gymnopédies
IS is the abbreviation for island
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Someone encounters a French composer on an island trip with his son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meets' looks like a verb of encountering; it means fulfils, as in meets a need.
explanation.definitionFit: To satisfy a requirement is to meet it, so satisfies and meets are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: A group on leave

blocks.note: taken as written
a band is a group, of musicians or people
taken as written

explanation.surface: A band of people is away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like a noun meaning time off; it is the verb, to desert.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon someone or something is to leave it behind for good.

clue.text: Opera singer's sad loss in seedy inn

indicators.note: something sad is in a sorry state, so the letters of the word beside it are messed up
seedy means shabby and run down, so the letters of the word beside it are knocked about
in places one group of letters inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A singer suffers a sad loss in a run-down pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Birgit Nilsson was a famous Swedish Wagnerian soprano. Both words are shuffled, and the rearranged 'loss' goes inside the rearranged 'inn'.
explanation.definitionFit: Birgit Nilsson was a celebrated Swedish dramatic soprano, so she is an example of an opera singer.

clue.text: Brag about doctor in pretentious speech

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes round the second

blocks.note: to boast is to brag
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A doctor shows off in an inflated, self-important speech.
explanation.walkthrough: MB stands for Bachelor of Medicine, the standard British medical degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombast is high-sounding but empty language, the stuff of pompous speeches.

clue.text: Beast in jazzy helmet

indicators.note: jazzy means wild and flashy, so the letters are livened up into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An animal wearing a flamboyant helmet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is part of the fodder, not a link or container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A basinet is a light, close-fitting medieval steel helmet, often with a pointed top.

clue.text: Memorable remarks made on the way out?

definitions.text: Memorable remarks made on the way out?

blocks.clueFragment: Memorable remarks made on the way out?
blocks.note: surface: witty comments someone makes as they leave a room
setter's reading: on the way out means dying, so these are celebrated sayings uttered at death

explanation.surface: Someone delivers a quotable parting shot as they head for the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the way out' suggests leaving a room; it means leaving life. The phrase is also used ironically of overconfident predictions.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the celebrated final utterances of people at the point of death.

clue.text: Not as many in Recife, we reckon

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the ends and starts of the words

explanation.surface: Someone estimates there are fewer of something in the Brazilian city of Recife.
explanation.definitionFit: Fewer is the comparative of few, meaning a smaller number of.

clue.text: This beast may charge one for lolly

blocks.note: first meaning: a large horned animal known for charging
second meaning: old British slang for money, as lolly is too

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone being billed; 'charge' is the animal's attack. Lolly is British slang for money, not a sweet, and the answer is older slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a large African or Asian horned animal and is also dated British slang for money.

clue.text: Mostly learned tricks in the Badger State

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: wise means learned, knowledgeable
cons are swindles or tricks
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some tricks were mostly picked up in a particular American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' reads as a verb (picked up); it is the adjective, knowledgeable.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisconsin's official nickname is the Badger State, after early lead miners who dug into hillsides.

clue.text: Jumping bail? I must give a reason

definitions.note: here an excuse offered in defence

indicators.note: jumping about moves things around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspect who skipped bail has to explain why.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere, and loosely any excuse offered to explain oneself.

clue.text: One held by flower girl

indicators.note: something held by another is gripped inside it

blocks.note: the rose is a flower
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A flower girl is holding something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower girl' reads as one phrase; 'girl' is the definition. I goes inside ROSE after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosie is a girl's name, so it is an example of a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Film noir too involved (American)

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and complicated, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
US is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A film noir is far too convoluted, says an American viewer.
explanation.walkthrough: Notorious is Hitchcock's 1946 thriller starring Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman.
explanation.definitionFit: Notorious is the title of a 1946 Alfred Hitchcock film, an example of a film.
